query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the propensity to form and maintain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C is governed by the ability of the dominant X element (Si or Al) to generate a high-entropy, single‐phase oxide that is structurally homogeneous and adherent. In a single-phase metallic solid-solution state, the uniform distribution of elements drives the formation of a coherent mixed-metal oxide (e.g., alumina or silica-like) that expands minimally and accommodates thermal stresses, whereas in multiphase alloys or when X is Mn, local compositional heterogeneities lead to the formation of unstable, non-cohesive oxides that crack or spall under oxidative or corrosive conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single-phase (homogeneous solid-solution) state, with X = Si, Mn, or Al.
generation.intervention: Modulate the identity of the X element and the phase state (single-phase vs. multiphase) of the alloy.
generation.conditions: Exposure to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: A coherent, high-entropy mixed-metal oxide layer that forms preferentially when the alloy is in a single-phase state and contains oxide-forming elements (Si or Al) that favor thermodynamically stable, slow-growing oxide compounds.
generation.mechanism: When the alloy is a single-phase solid solution, the uniformly distributed oxide-forming elements (particularly Si or Al) lead to the formation of a homogeneous protective oxide whose structure is stabilized by high configurational entropy. This coherent layer minimizes lattice mismatches and thermal expansion mismatch stresses, thereby reducing the likelihood of cracking or spallation. Conversely, in multiphase alloys or in alloys with Mn (which forms less stable oxides), heterogeneous oxidation kinetics promote phase separation within the oxide layer, leading to mechanical instabilities and eventual spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys containing Si or Al in a single-phase state will form a stable, coherent, and adherent oxide layer that persists at temperatures above 900 °C, whereas alloys with Mn or those with a multiphase structure will develop oxide scales that are prone to cracking or spallation under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: A multiphase CrFeCoNiMn alloy (or similarly composed alloy with Mn as the X element) exposed under identical oxidative/corrosive conditions, which is expected to develop unstable, non-coherent oxide scales.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys operating above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments, with the comparison strictly between single-phase and multiphase states and among different X elements (Si, Mn, Al).
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of oxide coherence, the thickness of the protective layer, and the kinetics of oxide layer formation may be sensitive to minor compositional variations and processing history. Additionally, quantitative differences in performance between Si- and Al-containing alloys need experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Si, Mn, and Al in both deliberately controlled single-phase and multiphase microstructures. Expose the alloys to controlled oxidative/corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C. Monitor the evolution, morphology, and coherence of the oxide layers over time using high-resolution in situ electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD), and surface analysis techniques.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate
Phase composition and crystallinity of the oxide (via XRD)
Microscopic evaluation of oxide coherence, adhesion, and spallation events (using electron microscopy)
Quantification of thermal expansion mismatch or strain in the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under high-temperature oxidative/corrosive conditions, single-phase alloys with Si or Al do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in oxide layer coherence and stability compared to multiphase alloys or Mn-containing alloys, or if multiphase alloys exhibit equal or superior oxide adherence, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Entropy-stabilized oxides

Abstract: Configurational disorder can be compositionally engineered into mixed oxide by populating a single sublattice with many distinct cations. The formulations promote novel and entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter where metal cations are incorporated in new ways. Here, through rigorous experiments, a simple thermodynamic model, and a five-component oxide formulation, we demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state. In the latter, cation distributions are proven to be random and homogeneous. The findings validate the hypothesis that deliberate configurational disorder provides an orthogonal strategy to imagine and discover new phases of crystalline matter and untapped opportunities for property engineering. The composition of oxide compounds controls many of their properties and electronic phases. Here, the authors show that entropy and configurational disorder can stabilize new phases of oxides, potentially enabling a better engineering of their properties.
